notes.meaning: The Lord of Hosts speaks judgment against the nation of Moab. Key towns like Nebo and Kiriathaim will be destroyed and captured by the invading army. Their high fortresses will be pulled down, showing that earthly defenses cannot protect against God.

Moab will no longer have anything to boast about. In Heshbon, the invading Babylonian commanders plot to wipe out Moab so it will no longer exist as a nation. The town of Madmen will also be struck dumb and silenced as the enemy sword chases down its people.
Loud screams of terror rise from the city of Horonaim. The invaders bring sudden ruin, and the people shout out in despair because of the great destruction falling on them.
The whole country of Moab is shattered by war. Even the young children scream aloud in terror as they experience the brutal cruelty of the invaders.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars translate the word for little ones as the town name Zoar, following ancient Greek translations.

notes.meaning: Fugitives climb the steep road to Luhith, weeping nonstop with every step. As they hurry down the other side toward Horonaim, the enemies hear their desperate cries of anguish echoing through the mountains.
The people are urged to run for their lives and leave everything behind. They must flee into the dry wilderness, becoming solitary and stripped of all wealth like a lonely desert bush.

Moab felt secure because of its strong fortresses, wealth, and local idol Chemosh. Because they trusted in these earthly things instead of the true God, their cities will fall, and the statue of Chemosh will be dragged into exile along with his priests and princes.
The Babylonian destroyer will advance against every single town in Moab, leaving no city untouched. The valleys and the flat tablelands will both be ruined just as the Lord declared.
The danger is so swift and intense that only wings like a bird could help the Moabites escape. Their cities will soon become empty ruins with nobody left to live in them.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern translations render the opening phrase as putting salt on Moab, seeing an ancient custom of sowing ruins with salt to mark complete destruction.

notes.meaning: A curse is declared on the soldiers if they do God's appointed work of judgment half-heartedly or hold back their swords from fighting. God uses Babylon as His instrument to punish Moab, and the judgment must be carried out completely.

differ.view: This verse is a strong figure of speech showing that Babylon's judgment would be total, not a general command promoting violence.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some modern commentators view this verse as a harsh addition by a later editor rather than the original words of Jeremiah.

notes.meaning: Moab is compared to wine that has sat undisturbed on its sediment for a long time. Because the nation had rarely faced invasion or gone into exile, its people grew proud and remained settled in their old sins.
God will send invaders who will act like workers tilting and emptying wine casks. They will turn Moab upside down, drive its people into exile, and smash its cities like broken clay jars.

Moab will be thoroughly embarrassed by its false god Chemosh when he fails to save them. This will be just like the northern kingdom of Israel, who was put to shame after trusting in the golden calf at Bethel.
The prophet challenges the proud boast of Moab's soldiers. They thought they were mighty heroes prepared for battle, but their human strength will not protect them against God's judgment.
Moab is ruined as enemy troops scale its walls and invade its towns. The best and strongest young soldiers are sent down to the slaughter by order of the Lord of Hosts, the true King.
The ruin of Moab will not be delayed. The trouble is already approaching and racing forward quickly to overtake them.

Neighboring nations and distant peoples who know Moab's fame are called to mourn over its fall. They will be stunned to see how such a mighty scepter and glorious staff of royal power could be completely broken.

The proud people of Dibon are told to step down from their seat of honor and sit in dry, parched misery. Though Dibon was famous for its flowing water, the Babylonians will tear down its strongholds and leave it stripped of all comfort.

The people living in the border town of Aroer are pictured standing by the road to watch for news. They anxiously stop every fleeing man and escaping woman to ask what terrible disaster has taken place in the cities to the north.
The fleeing refugees answer that Moab is disgraced and completely broken down. They tell the people by the river Arnon to wail loudly and announce that the whole nation is ruined.

God's judgment sweeps across the high tableland of Moab, striking town after town without stopping. Places like Holon, Jahzah, Mephaath, Dibon, Nebo, and Beth-diblathaim will all experience the enemy attack. This detailed list shows that no settlement on the plateau will be overlooked.

The judgment continues against Kiriathaim, Beth-gamul, Beth-meon, Kerioth, Bozrah, and every other town across Moab, whether far off or nearby. Naming so many places proves that the devastation is total, leaving no corner of the land safe from the invader.
